summary: Explains how AS112 name servers operate. Devices using private addresses, such as those in RFC 1918, sometimes send reverse DNS queries for them out to the Internet. AS112 servers answer those queries at a shared location so they do not overload the DNS root and other servers.

plainLanguage.summary: Lots of people ask the front desk about rooms that do not exist. A special helper desk answers with no such room, so the main desk is not bothered. AS112 is that helper desk for private Internet addresses, and this memo explains how to run one.

subtitle: How volunteers run a shared anycast sink that answers misdirected reverse-DNS queries for private addresses.

tldr.problem: Devices on sites that use private-use addresses often send reverse DNS lookups for those addresses out to the public DNS. No public server can give a useful answer, and the volume of such queries is large and growing.
tldr.mechanism: Independently operated AS112 nodes form an anycast cloud, announced from AS 112, that answers authoritatively for the relevant reverse zones with empty zone data. The RFC describes how to install and run such a node, covering routing, DNS software, testing and operations.
tldr.outcome: The queries are absorbed away from the IN-ADDR.ARPA authoritative servers. RFC 7534 obsoletes RFC 6304 and adds IPv6 transport, DNAME redirection and registry entries for the AS112 prefixes.

facts.label: TXT response guidance
facts.value: Fit within a 512-octet DNS over UDP datagram

today: RFC 7534 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 6304, and no later RFC is listed as replacing it. Compared with RFC 6304 it adds IPv6 transport, the DNAME redirection service, updated configuration guidance, and registry entries for the AS112 prefixes.

sections.title: Introduction: What AS112 Is For
sections.content:
Many sites connected to the Internet make use of IPv4 addresses that are not globally unique, for example the addresses designated in RFC 1918 for private use within individual sites. Devices in such environments may occasionally originate DNS queries, the so-called reverse lookups, corresponding to those private-use addresses. Since the addresses concerned have only local significance, it is good practice for site administrators to ensure that such queries are answered locally, but it is not uncommon for such queries to follow the normal delegation path in the public DNS instead of being answered within the site.

It is not possible for public DNS servers to give useful answers to such queries, and because of the wide deployment of private-use addresses and the continuing growth of the Internet, the volume of such queries is large and growing. The AS112 project aims to provide a distributed sink for these queries in order to reduce the load on the IN-ADDR.ARPA authoritative servers.

The project encompasses a loosely coordinated collection of independently operated nameservers. Each nameserver functions as a single node in an AS112 anycast cloud and is configured to answer authoritatively for a particular set of nominated zones. The project is named after the Autonomous System Number that was assigned to it.
sections.plainLanguage: A device inside a site asks the DNS to turn a private address into a name. That question has no public answer, but it still travels out to the public servers and costs everybody time. AS112 is a group of servers that gives the same empty answer, on purpose, close to the source.

sections.title: The AS112 Service and the Zones It Answers
sections.content:
The project currently uses direct delegation: zones whose traffic should go to an AS112 sink are delegated directly to AS112 nameservers, and each node is manually configured to answer appropriately for those zones. Nodes implemented in accordance with the guidance in this document continue to provide service for those zones.

RFC 7535 describes a different approach, DNAME redirection, in which queries towards specific zones are redirected to an empty zone hosted on the same AS112 servers. This document introduces that capability, which allows any zone administrator to sink query traffic in AS112 infrastructure without requiring changes to any AS112 node.

For direct delegation, AS112 nameservers answer authoritatively for the reverse zones corresponding to the RFC 1918 private-use netblocks: 10.IN-ADDR.ARPA, the range from 16.172.IN-ADDR.ARPA to 31.172.IN-ADDR.ARPA, and 168.192.IN-ADDR.ARPA. They also answer for 254.169.IN-ADDR.ARPA, which corresponds to the link local netblock 169.254.0.0/16 listed in RFC 6890. For DNAME redirection they answer authoritatively for the single zone EMPTY.AS112.ARPA. To aid identification of AS112 anycast nodes, each node also answers authoritatively for the zones HOSTNAME.AS112.NET and HOSTNAME.AS112.ARPA.

The relevant direct-delegation zones are delegated to two nameservers, BLACKHOLE-1.IANA.ORG at 192.175.48.6 and 2620:4f:8000::6, and BLACKHOLE-2.IANA.ORG at 192.175.48.42 and 2620:4f:8000::42. The server PRISONER.IANA.ORG at 192.175.48.1 and 2620:4f:8000::1 is listed in the MNAME field of the SOA records of the reverse zones served by AS112 nameservers and receives mainly dynamic update queries. The addresses of all these nameservers are covered by the IPv4 prefix 192.175.48.0/24 and the IPv6 prefix 2620:4f:8000::/48, and IPv6 transport for them has so far only been available for pre-production testing. For DNAME redirection, the single zone EMPTY.AS112.ARPA is delegated to the single nameserver BLACKHOLE.AS112.ARPA at 192.31.196.1 and 2001:4:112::1, covered by the IPv4 prefix 192.31.196.0/24 and the IPv6 prefix 2001:4:112::/48.
sections.plainLanguage: Every AS112 node answers for the same handful of reverse zones, and the zones are empty on purpose: the correct answer to a question about a private address is that there is no name. The zone data is identical everywhere, which is what makes the anycast arrangement work.

sections.title: Installing a New Node
sections.content:
Installing an AS112 node is relatively straightforward, though experience with inter-domain routing with BGP, DNS authoritative server operations and anycast distribution of DNS services may prove useful. Nodes may be located anywhere on the Internet, and for nodes intended to provide a public service it may well be advantageous to choose a location that is easily and cheaply reachable by multiple providers, such as an Internet Exchange Point. A node may advertise its service prefix to BGP peers for local use, analogous to a conventional peering relationship, or for global use, analogous to a customer relationship with one or more providers.

The platform should support either cloned loopback interfaces or the ability to bind multiple addresses to a single loopback interface, and the addresses of the nameservers are configured on these interfaces so that the DNS software can respond properly. A host acting as an AS112 anycast node should be dedicated to that purpose and not used to provide other services at the same time, because of the unpredictable and occasionally high traffic levels that AS112 nodes have been seen to attract. Startup scripts should start the components automatically after a reboot, in an order where routing software starts after DNS software and DNS software after the loopback interfaces are configured, and wrapper scripts should ensure that the service prefix is not advertised while the anycast addresses are not configured or the DNS software is not running.

Nodes signal the availability of AS112 nameservers using BGP: each node is a BGP speaker and announces the prefixes 192.175.48.0/24 and 2620:4f:8000::/48 with origin AS 112, while the IPv4 prefix 192.31.196.0/24 and the IPv6 prefix 2001:4:112::/48 support DNAME redirection. A node that is IPv4-only need not configure the IPv6 elements and vice versa; single-stack hosts can still contribute usefully and single-stack operation is not discouraged.

The DNS software is configured with one zone per reverse block, each served from a file holding nothing but a start of authority record and the two name server records. The memo gives the full text of these files, notes that the start of authority record should point at a mailbox suitable for receiving technical queries, and states that there should be no other resource records in the zones. The two hostname zones contain operational data for troubleshooting and measurement, and the responses to the TXT queries for those zones should fit within a 512-octet DNS over UDP datagram, so that they are available without EDNS0 support on the client. An optional LOC record at the zone apex gives the geospatial location of the node, and operational data should also be carried using NSID where the software supports it.
sections.plainLanguage: A new node is an ordinary server with two extra jobs: announce the AS112 addresses to the routing system, and answer the empty zones. The document gives the exact configuration files, and warns that the node should do nothing else, because it can attract a lot of traffic.

sections.title: Running and Monitoring a Node
sections.content:
AS112 nodes should be monitored to ensure they are functioning correctly, just as with any other production service, because a node that stops answering queries correctly can cause failures and timeouts in unexpected places and can lead to failures in dependent systems that are difficult to troubleshoot. A node that needs to go off-line, for planned maintenance or as part of diagnosing a problem, should stop advertising the AS112 service prefixes to its BGP peers, either by shutting down the routing software altogether or by causing the routing system to withdraw the route, so that query traffic is not blackholed while the DNS software is not functioning normally.

Use of the node should be measured in order to track long-term trends, identify anomalous conditions and ensure that the configuration is sufficient to handle the query load. The memo lists free monitoring tools, including bindgraph, dnstop and DSC, and suggests that operators take part in collection events as part of a larger coordinated effort to gather baselines, giving Day in the Life, coordinated by DNS-OARC, as an example.

It is good operational practice to notify the community of users that may fall within the reach of a new node before it is installed; at Internet Exchanges, local mailing lists usually exist for such announcements, and coordination with other AS112 operators is especially recommended for nodes intended to be globally reachable. Information pertinent to AS112 operations is maintained on the project's web site, and information about a node should also be published within the DNS, in the two hostname zones. Operators should also be aware of the measures described in RFC 6305 and direct site administrators appropriately.

On the future of the project, the memo notes that it is recommended practice for the operators of recursive nameservers to answer queries for zones served by AS112 nodes locally, so that queries never reach AS112 servers, but operational experience does not currently show a trend towards compliance. It is expected that some DNS software vendors will include default configuration implementing such measures, and if that software is widely deployed the query load received by AS112 nodes will decrease, but it is safe to assume it will not fall to zero. The use of DNAME redirection is new and informed by minimal operational experience; if it proves successful, the community might recommend retiring the original direct delegation service, though this document makes no such recommendation.
sections.plainLanguage: Running the node means watching it, taking it out of the routing system before you work on it, and telling the other operators when you add one. The document is also honest about the project's future: if recursive servers answered these questions locally, AS112 would have less work to do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Hosts should never normally send queries to AS112 servers, because queries relating to private-use addresses should be answered locally within a site. Hosts that send queries to AS112 servers may well leak information relating to private infrastructure to the public network, which could present a security risk, and AS112 operators may log this information, making it further subject to whatever security and privacy risks that might entail. These risks are orthogonal to the presence or absence of authoritative servers for these zones in the public DNS infrastructure.

Queries answered by AS112 servers are usually unintentional, so the responses are usually unexpected, and unexpected inbound traffic can trigger intrusion detection systems or alerts by firewalls. Operators of AS112 servers should be prepared to be contacted by operators of remote infrastructure who believe their security has been violated.

The deployment of AS112 nodes is very loosely coordinated compared to other services distributed using anycast, so the malicious compromise of a node and subversion of the data it serves are harder to detect through the lack of central management. Since it is conceivable that changing the responses to queries received by AS112 nodes might influence the behaviour of the hosts sending the queries, such a compromise might be used as an attack vector against private infrastructure. Operators should take appropriate measures to ensure that nodes are protected from compromise, such as would normally be employed for production nameserver or network infrastructure, and the guidance provided for root nameservers in RFC 2870 may be instructive.

The zones hosted by AS112 servers are not signed with DNSSEC, because given the distributed and loosely coordinated structure of the service, the zones could only be signed if the private key material used was effectively public, which would remove any security benefit from using those keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Two risks are named here. A site that sends these queries gives away a hint about its private network, and a node that was taken over could feed false answers back to those sites. The answer is ordinary operational care for a production server.
